html:
Al-Andalus was the name for the parts of the Iberian Peninsula, today Spain and Portugal, under Muslim rule from 711 to 1492. At its height it covered almost all of the peninsula; afterwards it shrank to the small kingdom of Granada.

It began with the Umayyad invasion of 711, when an army of Arabs and Berbers crossed from North Africa and destroyed the Visigothic kingdom within a few years. When the Abbasids overthrew the Umayyads in Damascus in 750, a surviving prince, Abd al-Rahman I, fled to Spain and set up an independent emirate at Córdoba. In 929 Abd al-Rahman III declared it the Caliphate of Córdoba, and Córdoba became one of the largest and most learned cities in Europe.

Phases:

  • 711 to 756: a province of the Umayyad Caliphate.
  • 756 to 1031: the emirate, then caliphate, of Córdoba.
  • After 1031: rival small kingdoms, the taifas. Toledo fell to Castile in 1085.
  • 1086 to 1200s: rule by the North African Almoravids and Almohads.
  • 1238 to 1492: the Nasrid Emirate of Granada, builders of the Alhambra.

Muslims, Christians and Jews lived side by side, not always peacefully. Its scholars, among them Averroes and Maimonides, passed Greek and Arabic science and philosophy into Latin Europe, much of it through translators at Toledo. The Christian Reconquista ended when Isabella and Ferdinand took Granada in 1492; the expulsion of the Jews followed that year.
sum: Al-Andalus was the name for the parts of the Iberian Peninsula, today Spain and Portugal, under Muslim rule from 711 to 1492. At its height it covered almost all of the peninsula; afterwards it shrank to the small kingdom of Granada.
